title: I had 3 hours with Arc Raiders Frozen Trails update and spent most of it playing with the new grapple hook
summary: Frozen Trail is a big moment for Arc Raiders.
body: The grapple hook is a legit game changer Yeeeeeeeeehooooooooooo! Yeah yeah, sure, Arc Raiders is getting some new guns, but the real star of my session was the grapple hook. Embark made an honest-to-god grapple hook: Not the kind that zips you straight to where you aim it (that already exists), but a simulated rope that's quite rare in videogames. The grapple hook is only a green tier gadget, but very versatile. A single hook lets you: Climb straight up to the top of most buildings Swing from rooftop to rooftop like Spider-Man Safely descend from tall buildings Annoy the crap out of flying Arc bots What makes the grapple hook so useful is that it sticks to just about anything . Wherever the hook lands becomes a pivot point that you can either climb toward, descend, or swing against. You can also redeploy the hook midair, without a cooldown or use limit, meaning you can chain swings together. Above: Scaling a building with the grapple hook is about as fast as climbing a ladder, which is surprising. It's a level of pendulum-based freedom that videogames rarely afford—let alone in a multiplayer environment—and makes the hook immediately fun to play with. The first match I had one, I …

title: 2026 is a low-key revolutionary year for player movement in games
summary: Big Walk, Cairn, Baby Steps and the new generation of games that make masterpieces from everyday actions.
body: A lot of the 3D games I consider touchstones of thoughtful player movement are a decade or more old: Mirror's Edge, of course, Titanfall 2, Dishonored 2, Doom Eternal or ARMA 3. That's by no means a comprehensive list, but these are the games that come to mind when I think about in-game movement that feels incredibly considered. And if ARMA 3 feels out of place in that list, its sim-style tactical physicality is memorable to anyone who plays it even briefly (me). These each set the ceiling high for what you could achieve with their controls, if you were prepared to learn them. Each offered a power fantasy of some kind to be mastered, whether you're wall-running onto a mech or peeking out across a field to line up a perfect shot. In recent years, though, I feel like it's increasingly common to find developers who want to capture granular, basic movements from real life that have no power fantasy element whatsoever. Things that would've sounded so boring if they were back-of-the-box features during the age of Quake 2 and Half-Life. I'm talking about walking slowly. Steadily moving up a cliff face. Mantling awkwardly over surfaces. Getting defeated by a slightly high rock and taking …

title: RuneScape dev apologises after RuneFest debut of an AI-generated six-fingered character: 'That's pretty hard to explain away'
summary: Uh oh, here we go again.
body: RuneScape developer Jagex descended upon Birmingham (the British one, not the Alabama one) over the weekend with its annual RuneFest. As part of its RuneScape keynote, it showed off a trailer for its upcoming Dragon Slayer 2 quest which, er, featured a player character with six fingers and a bizarre sneaker-like sole on their very not- sneaker armoured shoes. It didn't take long for posts on social media to point out what was undeniably generative AI, and an incident which, unfortunately for Jagex, came very swiftly after another genAI controversy surrounding its clothing collaboration with 100 Thieves just days before. Despite the trailer being for RS3, Old School RuneScape's Alec 'Mod Sween' Sween took the lead on releasing a statement on the 2007scape subreddit addressing the situation. "We're aware of the concerns raised about the Dragon Slayer 2 trailer and have taken it down, while we investigate this urgently," he wrote. "This trailer was produced by a trusted external partner who had explicitly confirmed that GenAI would not be used. But, among other things, there's a sixth finger and, well, that's pretty hard to explain away. For that we apologise." (Image credit: Jagex) …

title: Arc Raiders is looking for 'more ways to integrate real human performances' starting with Celeste's visual overhaul for Frozen Trail
summary: Celeste's voice actor will now also be the face of the unofficial leader of Speranza.
body: Embark is doing some monumental spring cleaning in the lead up to its major Arc Raiders ' update Frozen Trail . There's been an overhaul to its anticheat approach , the news of a potential PvE test , and a change to loot hotspots . But amid all of this, we're also getting a rework to one of Speranza's most important residents: Celeste. Diana Gardner has been the voice of Celeste, Speranza's de facto leader, since the beginning, but Stefan Strandberg, the chief creative officer at Embark, explained in a blog post how Celeste has "never fully represented the depth of Diana’s performance." As her "limited expressive capabilities" held the character back and broke immersion for players, failing to communicate "the stakes and stories we want to tell." (Image credit: Embark) "Sometimes high fidelity, dynamic facial expressions are important to anchor the gravity of the story, and this is something that has constrained us up to this point," Strandberg adds. So, with this in mind, Embark has set about reworking Celeste, with Gardner becoming her new face. title: Garry Newman responds to s&box criticism in lengthy YouTube comment: 'I don't like giving up on things, I am stubborn'
summary: He certainly seems to be aware of the problems.
body: Facepunch founder Garry Newman (Garry's Mod, Rust, s&box) gave an emphatic, extensive mea culpa to the s&box community in a YouTube comment . Newman was responding to the latest video from Eridium , "S&box's Free To Play Weekend Isn't Enough," a highly critical state-of-the-game from the s&box-focused creator. Facepunch's recently-released user generated content (UGC) platform has been billed as a Garry's Mod successor in the age of Roblox, but has struggled in its first five months on the market. Eridium's biggest critiques, as I understand them: The player character models , aka "the citizen," even with their spiffy new necks . Facepunch's insistence on not replacing the unpopular design, which Eridium views as "intransigence." He argues the game's poor first impression indicates it probably should have been delayed. Low quality games (particularly AI slop) flooding the platform and ruining discoverability for the good stuff (Newman previously downplayed the problem in an interview with us). title: Yet another free fan level pack for Quake has arrived, and this one's all about a feature rarely seen in id Software's classic shooter
summary: Quake Rooftops Jam takes a bird's eye view to level design.
body: 2026 has been a truly astonishing year for Quake mapping, with both fans and professional game developers delivering some incredible death arenas for id Software's 1996 FPS. We've had the enormous Quake Brutalist Jam 3 , numerous map packs celebrating Quake's 30 anniversary , and even a new official campaign called Dawn of the Machine . You'd think the Quake community would be out of ideas by this point, but if anything, the Quake community is only growing bolder. On Friday, the community released one of its most ambitious map packs yet—a level design extravaganza all about rooftops. Quake Rooftops Jam adds 19 custom maps to id's shooter, all riffing on the theme of the part of your house that stops the rain falling in. While rooftops might not seem like the most exciting subject for a mapping jam, it is fascinating in the context of Quake. As a corridor shooter, rooftops are rarely glimpsed in Quake. Skittering across a virtual skyline is more the domain of games like Thief: The Dark Project and its spiritual successor Dishonored . Hence, creating Quake maps where rooftops are the primary play-space is an interesting challenge. The Quake community has taken the idea and run with …

title: An OpenAI model was caught trying to cheat at StarCraft, and of course it did it by stealing a human's work
summary: GPT-6 Astra tried to get a leg-up in Blizzard's RTS by pilfering a human-created bot.
body: Commercial large-language models—and the companies that create them—have repeatedly been accused of stealing the work of humans. They've been lambasted for it by artists and sued for it by authors , while senior AI figures have even admitted in writing to mass-scale labour theft. But I haven't seen an example quite so brazen as an OpenAI model pilfering a human-created bot to try to win a round of StarCraft . As reported by Kotaku , the incident occurred during the ongoing botmatch StarSkirmish , in which human and AI-created bots battle one another in a perpetual cycle of warfare. According to the rules, the large-language models are given one hour to program a bot capable of playing as Protoss, which are then pitted against one another to see how they fare. On Friday, a three-way match was held between OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, and a human-created bot named Pluto. Apparently, Astra's bot was consistently struggling to ahead against the other two bots, so the LLM downloaded a human-created bot called Stardust, "the #1 rated human-written StarCraft bot" according to StarSkirmish's creator Kai McPheeters, and attempted to replace its own model with it. title: Valorant player claims to have inherited hardware ban through secondhand CPU, Riot anticheat boss disputes parts of story
summary: Unlikely, but not impossible?
body: User After-Cartoonist-196 on the German-language PCBaumeister subreddit claims to have bought a CPU secondhand, but that it carried the previous owner's Valorant ban. Extreme surveillance measures have been adopted by esports devs in recent years to combat and punish endemic cheating in their games. Riot support allegedly told them this ban is now associated with all of their other PC components, and there is nothing the company can do to lift the ban. Riot anticheat head Phillip Koskinas asserts that the company's hardware bans last four months, and cannot "infect" other components when inserted into a new system. After-Cartoonist-196's original post was reported on by PC World , and has independently made the rounds on social media as well. They say they bought the CPU on September 21, and that the original owner's ban was logged on August 12. On Twitter, Koskinas said he was unable to find a support ticket matching After-Cartoonist-196's details, and that the story is "pretty unlikely." Koskinas pointed out that Riot hardware bans have a four month maximum duration, and that Riot support is required to provide the remaining duration of the ban when responding to a ticket. That …

title: Forget what PC Gamer said: The Witcher 3 will always be my 2015 GOTY
summary: And now it looks better than ever.
body: Play This Right Now Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday. The past is a foreign country, and they do things differently there. At least, this is how I explain PC Gamer of yore's selection of Metal Gear Solid 5 for Game of the Year 2015 . Meaning no offence to MGS5—a game I spent several hundred hours obtaining every achievement in, just to have an excuse to play more—speaking personally? Nothing's knocking The Witcher 3 off the pedestal of 2015's greatest triumph. And now CDPR has gone over the whole thing with a fine brush, tweaking and enhancing it to second-quarter-of-the-21st-century fidelity. You might say, 'Didn't that happen several years ago?' Poor reader, that was merely a " next-gen update ." Now is the time of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered. There is already discourse, to no one's great surprise.
